subject: EdgeCloud dedicated capacity: throughput model & GPU fleet recommendation
messages:
From: Jane Williams <jane.w@edgecloud.com>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 03 Nov 2025 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Dedicated capacity sizing for EdgeCloud inference

Marcus —

Thanks for the quick sync earlier. To follow up, we need a formal sizing recommendation for a Dedicated deployment (customer-owned VPC) for our on-device analytics feature. High-level workload: ~1,200 peak concurrent users on our web UI, expected peak 1,800 requests/minute (30 req/sec) during promotional windows, average generated tokens per response ~120 tokens, typical model: we will evaluate 13B and 70B variants. SLO target is 95p latency under 400ms for the first token and 95p end-to-end response under 1.5s for typical replies.

Key asks:
- Recommended GPU fleet size for each model variant to meet SLO with 25% headroom
- Tokens/sec assumptions per GPU and back-of-envelope math
- Autoscale/overflow strategy and how quickly you can spin up burst capacity
- Any warm-up / KV cache recommendations for launch day spikes

Can you send a concise model (spreadsheet + summary) we can attach to our procurement/infra packet? Procurement (procurement@edgecloud.com) will need estimated monthly committed cost as well.

Thanks,
Jane
CTO, EdgeCloud

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Jane Williams <jane.w@edgecloud.com>
Cc: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 04 Nov 2025 11:46:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity sizing for EdgeCloud inference

Jane — thanks for the clear parameters. I attached a compact model (tokens_per_sec_model.xlsx) and a one-page capacity summary (capacity_plan_v2.pdf). High-level summary below — numbers include a 25% operational headroom by default; we can tune to your procurement targets.

Assumptions we used (configurable in the spreadsheet):
- Peak requests: 30 req/sec (1,800 req/min)
- Avg generated tokens per request: 120 tokens
- Target steady-state SLOs: 95p first-token <400ms, 95p full-response <1.5s

Model throughput figures (observed on A100 80GB / Redwood runtime, conservative picks):
- redwood-13b-quant (int8-like profile): ~200 tokens/sec per GPU
- redwood-13b-fp16: ~320 tokens/sec per GPU (higher perf, more memory)
- redwood-70b-quant: ~28 tokens/sec per GPU
- redwood-70b-fp16: ~45 tokens/sec per GPU

Sizing math (peak):
- Total tokens/sec at peak = requests/sec * tokens/request = 30 * 120 = 3,600 tokens/sec
- GPUs required (redwood-13b-quant) = ceil(3,600 / 200) = 18 GPUs -> +25% headroom = 23 GPUs
- GPUs required (redwood-13b-fp16) = ceil(3,600 / 320) = 12 GPUs -> +25% = 15 GPUs
- GPUs required (redwood-70b-quant) = ceil(3,600 / 28) = 129 GPUs -> +25% = 161 GPUs
- GPUs required (redwood-70b-fp16) = ceil(3,600 / 45) = 80 GPUs -> +25% = 100 GPUs

Latency fit (spot-check):
- For 13B-quant, 200 tokens/sec -> 120 tokens take 0.6s to generate; first-token median ~80-120ms depending on batching; with continuous batching and caching we expect 95p first-token ~<350ms and full-response ~<900ms (fits your 1.5s target).
- For 70B variants, token latency is much higher per token; even fp16 would be borderline for tight first-token SLO without aggressive batching and caching.

Operational notes / headroom rationale:
- We recommend reserving at least 10–15% of capacity for KV cache warm-up and transient spikes (included in the 25% headroom).
- Autoscale burst: Dedicated supports pre-warmed burst pools (minutes to spin-up) and cloud-backed transient capacity within ~5–15 minutes depending on region and agreement. For promotional windows, we recommend scheduled scaling + a 20% pre-warm lane.
- Fallback strategy: we can configure policy to route to a smaller-variant (13B-quant) or to a cached summary response when capacity is saturated.

Next steps we suggest:
1) Confirm preferred model variant (13B vs 70B) — we recommend 13B-quant for cost/latency balance.
2) If procurement wants committed capacity pricing, we’ll map the GPU counts above to a reserved monthly MSRP and a transit/overflow hourly rate.
3) We’ll deliver a one-page SLO mapping that shows 50/95/99p latencies per variant for your runbook.

Files attached: tokens_per_sec_model.xlsx (detailed calc), capacity_plan_v2.pdf (executive summary), redwood_variant_latency_matrix.csv (measurement matrix).

Let me know if you want me to present these numbers to procurement this week.

— Marcus
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Marcus / team —

2) Is there a recommended autoscale cooldown and minimum pre-warmed lanes you recommend for promotional spikes?

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: procurement@edgecloud.com, Jane Williams <jane.w@edgecloud.com>
Cc: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 07 Nov 2025 17:42:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity sizing for EdgeCloud inference

Team — quick follow-up with procurement numbers and an ops note from Olga (copied). See short answers below; I also uploaded a pricing snapshot to the Drive link.

Procurement answers (13B-quant baseline):
- Estimated committed monthly (15 GPU reserve): $XXX,XXX/month (reserved discounted rate) — full table in attached pricing sheet.
- Incremental hourly burst (on-demand) per GPU: $Y.YY/hr (region-dependent).
- Recommended min pre-warmed lane for promo windows: 20% of baseline reserved capacity (for 15 GPUs baseline -> 3 GPUs pre-warm) + ability to spin additional transient GPUs in 5–15 minutes.
- Autoscale cooldown: 3–5 minutes for scale-down, scale-up can be fast but depends on cloud placement. We recommend scheduled scale-ups 10–15 minutes before expected spike plus dynamic autoscale.

Latency caveats if starting at 15 GPUs and autoscaling the rest:
- During initial ramp, you'll see higher 95p full-response times (likely 1.2–2.5s) if most requests hit uncached cold model instances. After warm-up and KV cache population, latency should fall back to within SLO for the 13B-quant variant.
- We recommend a staged rollout: start with 15 reserved, add 5 GPUs as short-term buffer, and use scheduled scaling for predictable promos. That buys you predictable billing while keeping peak latencies controlled.

Internal ops note (Olga):
> Marcus / Jane — also call out that we should optimize batch windows for 13B-quant to reduce per-token overhead; a 20–40ms batching window for web traffic tends to preserve first-token SLOs while improving throughput. Plan for a cache-grace period after deploy (~30–45 minutes) for KV priming.

Next: I can hand this to our sales pricing lead for a formal quote (line items: 15 GPU reserved, 8 GPU burst pool, on-demand overflow). Shall I proceed?

— Marcus

Adding a quick operational tweak:
- Recommend quantized 13B as GA launch model; reserve a small pool (2–4 GPUs) running fp16 13B for high-quality samples or specific enterprise customers.
- Include a plan to stage KV cache priming: run a warm-up job 45–60 minutes before peak with synthetic traffic (we can provide the runner).
- For the SLO-runbook, include a fallback policy: if queued tokens > X for >Y seconds, drop to summarized response (explained in the SOW).
